newsitem.title: NORWAY: Brundtland, Norway's veteran premier, to quit.
newsitem.headline: Brundtland, Norway's veteran premier, to quit.

text.p: Prime Minister Gro Harlem Brundtland, who has dominated Norwegian politics for 15 years, announced on Wednesday she would resign to give her Labour Party a fresh start for next year's election.

The surprise announcement that 57-year-old Brundtland would quit on Friday immediately led to speculation that she would seek a top job at the United Nations, possibly aiming to succeed Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali.

Brundtland, evasive as always on whether she wants to pursue an international career, told a news conference she would continue to work as a member of parliament but added, amid laughter, that "nothing is alien to me".
In a carefully managed handover of power, Brundtland said in a statement that Labour Party leader Thorbjoern Jagland would succeed her as prime minister on Friday.

Brundtland said economic and other policies of the oil-rich Scandinavian nation of 4.3 million would remain unchanged under Jagland, who was appointed party leader in 1992 and has since been groomed as her successor.
Jagland is widely seen as leaning more to the left than Brundtland. But commentators say that, as party leader for four years, he is not likely to change course when he is premier.
Parliament is locked in debate on the Labour minority government's 1997 budget proposals. The opposition is seeking to increase spending and the government is trying to defend tight fiscal policies.

"I don't think Brundtland's resignation will change the budget debate in any significant way," said financial analyst Oeystein Stephansen of Oslo-based S-E Banken. "This is more of a leadership issue in the Labour Party."

Brundtland, known internationally for strong-minded views, said it was time to make clear "who would be at the helm of a Norwegian Labour government beyond this parliamentary election (in September 1997) and possibly into the next century".
Speculation has centered for a year on whether Brundtland would step down before the next general election. If so, observers had expected her to quit at a Labour Party congress next month.
The prime minister's announcement that she would submit the resignation on Friday took parliament by surprise. The session was adjourned after she finished her brief statement.
Brundtland, a tough political survivor, became Norway's first woman prime minister in 1981. She has been the country's dominant politician ever since, despite periods out of power.
But Brundtland, who has been in office for a total of 10 years, has taken a mauling from the traditionally sympathetic Norwegian press in recent months.

A half-page cartoon last week in the best-selling daily Dagbladet depicted the stocky prime minister as a bloated monarch surrounded by tired courtiers paying little or no attention to any of her announcements.

"I have a clear conscience," Brundtland told the news conference. "I feel that I have done a reasonably good job over a number of years. I feel that I can safely hand over the responsibility to others."
She said she decided a year ago to quit ahead of the party congress so Labour could devote its time entirely to the party programme and next year's election campaign.
